CLASS 31 · PRESCHOOL AGES 4–5

Science, Nature & Discovery

Age 4–5 YearsClass 31Adventures 30 science gamesSubjects Plants · animals · weather · light · sound

Explore plants, animals, weather, habitats, light, sound, water, and everyday science through playful discovery activities. Thirty draw-on-the-picture adventures — every one played on its own science illustration, with plain written instructions and a printable worksheet twin in the Science worksheet library.

Predictions to make, insects to count, magnets to test, habitats to match and one graduation lab — every question is one big picture your child draws right on.

Meet the adventures ↓Science is best in short, curious sittings.

TAKE IT OFF SCREEN

Science play at the kitchen table.

Drop a spoon and a cork in the bath (04). Melt an ice cube on the windowsill (15). Raid the recycling with a magnet (11, 21). Grow a bean in a jam jar (01, 18). Blow a dandelion and watch the seeds fly (22). Every game here has a real experiment hiding inside it — the picture is the invitation.

SUPPORTING RESOURCE · EXPLORE SCIENCE FLASHCARDS

Explore the Science Flashcards.

The thirty adventures above teach HOW to explore — predict, test, draw and try again. The flashcard collection teaches WHAT each idea means: what an ant trail is, why rain falls, where a shadow comes from, how a magnet pulls without touching.

Every card gives grown-ups a plain-words why-it-matters note and a two-minute experiment to try at home. Open one before or after its matching adventure — the words make the play make sense.

A NOTE FROM THE PRINCIPAL

For the grown-ups.

Early science is predicting, testing and talking — never a quiz. Every game here asks your child to commit to a guess first, and every miss brings a friendly explanation instead of a penalty. The say-lines are written so YOU can steal them for bath time and walks.

The worksheets are the paper twins — the same experiments with room to predict, circle and draw. Browse the science worksheets and print the adventure your child loved. Playing games never marks a class complete; only real game finishes do, and only for the child chosen in My Classroom.

MEASURE LIKE A SCIENTIST

Class 42 · Measuring & Money.

Class 31 predicts, tests and writes down what happened — and the Measuring & Money class hands the scientist a toolkit: twenty-eight printable math cards for ages 4–5 with the ruler, the height chart, the balance scale, the timer words and the money math that pays for the materials. Every card prints straight from the class page — measuring is where math and science hold hands.

FROM EXPERIMENTS TO THE STARS

Class 43 · Our Earth & Space.

Class 31 predicts, tests and writes down what happened — and the Our Earth & Space class looks all the way up: twenty-four printable space flashcards for ages 4–5 with the planets, the spinning Earth, the weather, rockets and astronauts, and the stars. Every card downloads and prints straight from the class page with its sky words and a way to try it today right beneath the image.

FROM DISCOVERY TO DAILY HABITS

Class 47 · Caring for Our Planet.

Class 31 discovers how the world works — seeds sprout, water cycles, magnets pull — and the Caring for Our Planet class turns those discoveries into habits a four-year-old can do before dinner: thirty printable eco flashcards for ages 4–5, from planting a tree and rescuing a bee to sorting the recycling and switching off the lights, every card downloading and printing straight from the class page.

THE PLANT SCIENCE, NAMED

Class 48 · Plants & How They Grow.

Class 31 runs the experiments — seeds sprouting in jars, sink or float, the water cycle — and the Plants & How They Grow class names the plant science those experiments ride on: forty-one printable plant flashcards for ages 4–5, from a seed cracking open to the bee’s pollination errand, every card downloading and printing straight from the class page.

LOOK UP, THEN LOOK & LEARN

The sky words come back down in Look & Learn.

Moon, star, cloud, raindrop, sun, leaf and acorn — the everyday science of this class — come back as pictures in Look & Learn, fifteen cards with a look-and-say move on every one: point at the moon, stretch toward the sun, match something green to the leaf. It is the gentlest way to hand this class to a toddler sibling tonight.

TEACHER’S LESSON

How this class is taught.

By the end of this class: your child has met all 35 cards in Science, Nature & Discovery, said each word with you and tried one small activity from the lesson.

  1. 01
    Welcome

    “Hello! Today we are learning about Science, Nature & Discovery. We have 35 cards, and we will look at them one at a time.”

    How: Sit side by side with the cards in front of you. Keep your voice warm and unhurried, and let your child touch the cards.

  2. Cards 1–10
  3. 02
    Card 1 · Ant

    “Look — one crumb, many ants! Where do you think they are all going?”

    How: Find an ant trail on the pavement and drop a tiny breadcrumb a few steps away. Watch how long it takes for the first scout to find it — then the second, and the tenth. No touching, just watching.

  4. 03
    Card 2 · Bee

    “Why is the bee visiting that flower? Do you think the flower says thank you?”

    How: Find two or three flowers with bees on them, stand back and count visits: which flower do the bees like best? Talk about colors and smells — from a distance, hands in pockets.

  5. 04
    Card 3 · Snail

    “Where does a snail sleep? Look — it carries its house everywhere it goes!”

    How: Morning snail hunt after rain: find one, watch which way it goes, and follow the shiny slime trail backwards. Is the trail always one line? What happens when the snail meets a wall?

  6. 05
    Card 4 · Spider

    “How does the spider know dinner has arrived? The web rings like a dinner bell!”

    How: Find a web after rain or early dew — it sparkles and shows its pattern. Watch from a distance: has anything been caught? Never touch the web; it took the spider hours to build.

  7. 06
    Card 5 · Butterfly Begins as a Caterpillar

    “Was the butterfly always a butterfly? What was it before it had wings?”

    How: Go on a caterpillar hunt: look under and along leaves in the garden or park. Found one? Look at it together, count its segments — and leave it exactly where it is. It has eating to do.

  8. 07
    Card 6 · Butterfly Life Cycle

    “Egg, caterpillar, chrysalis, butterfly — can you put the four stages in order with your finger?”

    How: Draw the four stages as four circles and let your child fill each one. Then hunt for a real chrysalis under leaves and fences — it looks like a tiny dried leaf, and that is exactly the point.

  9. 08
    Card 7 · Frog

    “The baby frog swims before it hops! What changes as a tadpole grows up?”

    How: Visit a pond in spring and look for jelly-like frogspawn or tiny tadpoles — watch, do not take. At home, jump like a frog from crouch to crouch: what do legs do that tails cannot?

  10. 09
    Card 8 · Fish

    “We breathe air with lungs — how does a fish breathe under water? Watch its gills!”

    How: Watch a goldfish or aquarium fish for a minute: the gill covers open and close like tiny doors. Count the opening beats in ten seconds — faster than you breathe? Slower?

  11. 10
    Card 9 · Bones

    “Feel your shin, your ribs, your knuckles — that is your skeleton, saying hello!”

    How: Skeleton feel-hunt: press gently and find five hard places — shin, ribs, elbow, knee, skull. Then bend: which parts bend (joints!) and which stay straight?

  12. 11
    Card 10 · Eyes

    “Close your eyes for three seconds — what changed? What did your ears start doing?”

    How: Blink-count game: try not to blink for as long as you can (it is hard!), then blink fast ten times. Try a short "ears only" moment with eyes closed — what do you notice that you usually miss?

  13. Cards 11–20
  14. 12
    Card 11 · Heart

    “Put your hand on your chest — that thump-thump is your heart working right now!”

    How: Jump ten times, then feel your heartbeat with a hand on the chest: fast! Rest until it slows down. Jump again and compare. A toy stethoscope — or a grown-up’s ear — makes it even better.

  15. 13
    Card 12 · Teeth

    “Bite like a rabbit, tear like a lion, grind like a horse — which teeth are you using?”

    How: Mirror dinner: bite an apple slice with the front teeth, then chew with the back teeth. Count how many teeth you can see in the mirror, and check the back ones got brushed too.

  16. 14
    Card 13 · What Plants Need

    “What would happen to a plant with no water? No light? Let’s find out — gently!”

    How: Grow two beans in jars on the windowsill and water both — then put ONE inside a dark cupboard for a few days. Water both, compare every day, and let your child announce the verdict.

  17. 15
    Card 14 · Seed

    “What is hiding inside this little seed? Let’s plant it and catch it waking up!”

    How: Soak a bean overnight (it swells!), then plant it against the inside wall of a clear jar with wet cotton so the roots are watchable. Mark the jar with the date and draw what appears.

  18. 16
    Card 15 · Tree Parts

    “Point to the roots, the trunk, the leaves — which part drinks? Which part cooks?”

    How: Tree-hug inspection: find a big tree, find its roots (they peek above soil!), rub bark with paper and a crayon, and collect three different fallen leaves. One tree, three discoveries.

  19. 17
    Card 16 · Cactus

    “It almost never rains in the desert — how does a cactus save water for later?”

    How: Sponge comparison: soak one sponge, leave another dry, and squeeze both — that is what a full cactus stem feels like inside. Then look at a cactus picture: where ARE the leaves? (The spines!)

  20. 18
    Card 17 · Mushroom

    “Where should we look for mushrooms — the sunny sandpit or the rainy corner under the tree?”

    How: After rain, go on a mushroom spot-walk: check shady grass, damp soil, old logs. Golden rule: LOOK, never touch or taste — wild mushrooms are grown-up territory. Photograph or draw instead.

  21. 19
    Card 18 · Pond Habitat

    “Who lives in this small home? Sit still and count every living thing you spot.”

    How: Pond-sit counting: at a safe distance from the edge, sit for five quiet minutes and tally everything alive — swimmers, floaters, jumpers, things on the surface. Stillness finds more than poking.

  22. 20
    Card 19 · Cloud

    “What are clouds made of? Can you catch one? (Breath on a cold window — you just made a tiny one!)”

    How: Cloud watch: lie back and find shapes — a bunny, a boat. Then breathe on a cold mirror or window and look at the mist: tiny water drops, just like a cloud, made by you.

  23. 21
    Card 20 · Rain

    “Where does rain come from? Up in the cloud, the tiny drops held hands until they got too heavy!”

    How: Be a rain reporter from the window: how heavy is it — drips, drops or pouring? Then map the puddles after: which puddle is biggest, and how long until the sun drinks it back?

  24. Cards 21–30
  25. 22
    Card 21 · Rain Helps Plants

    “The garden is drinking! What happens to the plants when it rains for a whole week?”

    How: After rain, take a leaf-and-garden tour: look at leaves wearing raindrops, and peek at the soil — dark, damp and drinking. Then check whether the puddles near your plants are still there tomorrow.

  26. 23
    Card 22 · Rainbow

    “How many colors can you count? Red, orange, yellow, green, blue... what comes next?”

    How: Make your own: stand with the sun BEHIND you and mist a hose or spray into the air — a small rainbow appears in the water. Try it from the same spot on a sunny morning or after rain.

  27. 24
    Card 23 · Wind

    “Can you see the wind? How do you KNOW it is there? What told you?”

    How: Become wind detectives: find five things the wind is moving — leaves, flags, hair, clouds, washing. Then make a paper streamer and hold it up: still air hangs it down, wind lifts it.

  28. 25
    Card 24 · Ice

    “Where did the ice cube go? It did not disappear — it melted! Can you find it?”

    How: Freeze water into cubes, then hold one in a warm hand and one on a cold plate — which melts first? Watch the puddle it leaves: the ice did not vanish, it turned back into water.

  29. 26
    Card 25 · Rock

    “Is this rock the same as that one? Feel them — bumpy, smooth, heavy, light?”

    How: Rock collection: gather five rocks and pebbles (parks, paths, beaches), then sort them your own way — by color, by texture, by size. Which one is the smoothest? Which is the heaviest for its size?

  30. 27
    Card 26 · Sun

    “What does the sun give us? Feel your cheek in the sunshine — warmth! Open your eyes — light!”

    How: Warm-wall test: put one hand on a sunny wall and one on a wall in the shade. Which hand is warmer? That warmth travelled 150 million kilometres — from a star — to reach your hand.

  31. 28
    Card 27 · Moon

    “Does the moon make its own light? No — it is a mirror catching the sun!”

    How: Moon diary: look for the moon every evening and draw its shape — crescent, half, full. Some nights it hides! Check before bed AND in the morning: the moon sometimes works the day shift.

  32. 29
    Card 28 · Day and Night

    “Where does the sun go at night? Nowhere — WE turn away from it! The Earth is slowly spinning right now.”

    How: Flashlight Earth: shine a torch on a ball or apple — the lit side is day, the dark side is night. Slowly turn the ball: watch day move across it. Now spin yourself once — that took a day’s worth.

  33. 30
    Card 29 · Volcano

    “What is inside a volcano? Melted rock called lava — hot enough to glow! What do YOU think happens when a mountain gets too hot inside?”

    How: Kitchen eruption with a grown-up: build a mountain of dough around a cup, add a spoon of baking soda, pour in vinegar — and step back. Then compare: bubbly foam lava, real lava, both flow downhill.

  34. 31
    Card 30 · Dinosaur Fossil

    “Nobody ever saw a living dinosaur — so how do we know them? We read their buried bones!”

    How: Cookie excavation: give your child a toothpick and a chocolate-chip cookie — the chips are fossils, the cookie is rock. Dig out every chip without breaking it. Slow hands win; that is exactly what palaeontologists do.

  35. Cards 31–35
  36. 32
    Card 31 · What Magnets Attract

    “Will it stick? Guess FIRST — the spoon? the coin? the toy car? — then test it!”

    How: Magnet hunt: take a fridge magnet around the house and test ten things — spoons, coins, keys, toys, zips, the door handle. Sort them into two piles: STICKS and NO. What do the stickers have in common?

  37. 33
    Card 32 · Magnet Force

    “Feel that! The magnet pushed my hand away without touching — can you feel the invisible push?”

    How: Two-magnet game: feel pull when opposite ends meet and push when the same ends meet. Then slide a piece of paper between a magnet and a paperclip — the magnet still works THROUGH it!

  38. 34
    Card 33 · Sound

    “Put your fingers on your throat and hum — feel that buzzing? You ARE the sound!”

    How: Rice drum: stretch a balloon skin or cling film over a bowl, sprinkle dry rice on top, and tap a pot loudly beside it — watch the rice jump with every boom. The jumping is the vibration, made visible.

  39. 35
    Card 34 · Shadow

    “Where did your shadow go? Stand in the sun — there it is! Now jump — does it jump too?”

    How: Hand puppets: in a darkish room, shine a torch on the wall and make bird and dog shadows with your hands. Then stand outside at noon and in the evening — is your shadow the same length? Measure it against a chalk line.

  40. 36
    Card 35 · Feather

    “Why does a feather float down slowly while a stone drops fast? Which one would you rather be?”

    How: The drop race: from the same height, drop a feather and a stone (or a coin) — the feather floats, dances and lands last, because the air catches every strand. Then find a real feather on a walk and look at the tiny hooks.

  41. 37
    Practice

    “Now you are the teacher! Pick any card and tell me what it is.”

    How: Let your child choose the card and say the word in their own way. Teaching someone else is the strongest way to remember.

  42. 38
    Check

    “Can you find Ant? Now show me Pond Habitat.”

    How: A point, a fetch or the word all count as a pass. If they are unsure, name it for them and try again another day — there are no scores and no pressure.

  43. 39
    Well done

    “Well done! Today we met 35 cards. Let us look for one of them at home.”

    How: End on a win, then spot one of the words in real life today. Meeting it again in the real world is what makes it stay.

Read the script while you show the cards — the say-lines are yours to say out loud and the how-lines are the activity behind each step. Skip, shorten or repeat anything: the class bends to your child, never the other way round.
